Kangling (Tibetan rkang-gling, literally 'leg flute' or 'leg-bone horn') is an aerophone horn used in Tibetan Buddhism, Hornbostel–Sachs number 423.121.11. It is traditionally made from the shinbone or thighbone of a dead person or of a respected teacher, and wood may also be used; today a metal imitation of a leg bone is common, with turquoise, coral, gold, silver or copper bands at both ends. It is blown, and in chöd (a Tibetan Buddhist rite) it is used only outdoors and together with drum and bell; it is also used at funerals and in tantric rites conducted by a chöpa (the rite's performer).

What can be confirmed is the basic action: in tantric rites or rites for cutting through ego-clinging it sounds as a blown horn, usually with hand drum and bell and only outdoors; the practitioner blows it as a gesture of fearlessness, to summon hungry ghosts and demons and as an act of cutting through ego-clinging.
其发声原理属气鸣，以吹奏骨管或仿骨管体发声；来源未载具体音色、音域与音量控制方式: Its principle is that of an aerophone: it sounds by blowing a bone tube or a tube imitating bone. The source does not record its specific timbre, range or means of controlling volume. Compared with trumpets and horns, the material stresses that it is made of human bone or a metal imitation, is used in tantric rites and outdoor ceremonies, is usually played together with drum and bell, and serves as a ritual implement for summoning hungry ghosts and cutting through ego-clinging.

脛骨號見於藏傳佛教，主要用於施身法與由施身法行者主持的喪禮；其使用限於戶外施身法: The kangling is found in Tibetan Buddhism and is used mainly for chöd and for funerals conducted by a chöd practitioner; its use is confined to chöd held outdoors, together with the chöd drum and bell. In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries Chopa Lugu of Kathok Monastery was famous for blowing a bone horn at night on a pilgrimage, to the annoyance of the merchants travelling with him, and was later called 'the chöd yogi who split the Chinese cliff'. In later times, besides human leg bone or thighbone, wood is also found, and today metal is often used in the shape of a leg bone, with turquoise, coral, gold, silver or copper bands at both ends; it is blown in tantric rites as a symbol of impermanence.
